c.tagline: Gateway to the Amalfi Coast, with a medieval heart and a palm-lined seafront.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered with fixed supplements for the airport and Amalfi Coast runs; agree the fare in advance for longer coastal trips.

emergency.note: 112 is the single EU emergency number connecting to police, fire and ambulance; 118 reaches medical emergencies directly.

hood_landmark.Centro Storico: Via dei Mercanti Salerno old town

avoid.reason: Keep an eye on bags around the train station and port and on packed Amalfi Coast buses and ferries in summer.

hood_desc: Salerno's medieval heart, a warren of alleys along Via dei Mercanti leading to the Duomo (Cathedral of San Matteo) and up toward the Arechi Castle; best for visitors who want history, character and lively evening spots on foot.
The palm-lined seafront promenade with gardens, bars and gelaterie facing the Gulf of Salerno; central and scenic, great for strolls and dining with a sea view.
The busy area around Salerno Centrale train station and the Corso Vittorio Emanuele shopping street; convenient for onward trains and ferries and packed with mid-range hotels.
A residential seafront district west of the center with a small beach and local restaurants; quieter and handy for the port, suiting travelers wanting a calmer base.
A largely residential eastern neighborhood near the marina and Arechi stadium, with everyday shops and eateries; a low-key, local place to stay away from the tourist crowds.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:30 AM to about 10:30 PM; regional trains and the urban metro line run longer, and taxis cover the late-night gap.
transit.note: Salerno is served by Busitalia Campania (formerly CSTP) city and regional buses, a short urban metro/rail line, mainline Trenitalia trains at Salerno Centrale, and seasonal passenger ferries along the Amalfi Coast from the Molo Manfredi terminal.
transit.pay: Buy bus tickets in advance at tabaccherie, newsstands or machines and validate on board; single urban fares are cheap, and train and ferry tickets are bought at stations or the port.

bus: SITA Sud regional coaches to the Amalfi Coast
ferry: Seasonal ferries to Amalfi, Positano, Capri and Cetara (Molo Manfredi)

transit.m: Shuttle bus to Salerno Centrale station (~40 min)
Taxi to the city center (25-30 min)

tip.r: A cover charge (coperto) is usually added; tipping beyond that is not expected, though rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is appreciated.

food.name: Scialatielli ai frutti di mare
food.desc: Short, thick hand-cut egg pasta from the Amalfi Coast tossed with clams, mussels, prawns and cherry tomatoes.

places.name: Trattoria Pummarola 'ncoppa
places.note: Traditional seafood cooking and the city's benchmark plate of scialatielli.

places.name: Osteria Canali
places.note: Small home-style osteria in the old lanes, seasonal Campanian dishes at fair prices.

places.name: Il Cavatappi
places.note: Popular pasta-and-wine spot, reliably busy with locals in the evening.

food.name: Pizza and calzone
food.desc: Campanian pizza with a puffed, blistered rim, plus stuffed calzoni with ricotta, salami and black pepper.

places.name: Vicolo della Neve
places.note: Historic tavern-pizzeria, celebrated for its stuffed calzoni and old-Salerno atmosphere.

places.name: Criscemunno
places.note: Light-dough pizza in a former convent, with a terrace facing the cathedral facade.

places.name: Opificio
places.note: Modern pizza laboratory working with long fermentation and local toppings.

food.name: Mozzarella di bufala del Cilento
food.desc: Milky buffalo mozzarella made the same morning in the plains south of the city, eaten plain with bread and olive oil.

places.name: Tenuta Vannulo
places.note: Organic buffalo farm with its own dairy, cafe and gelato; book ahead in season.

places.name: Caseificio Barlotti
places.note: Long-established dairy beside the Greek temples, selling mozzarella made that day.

places.name: Alimentari on Via dei Mercanti
places.note: Old-town delis keep fresh buffalo mozzarella and Cilento cheeses for picnics.

food.name: Alici di Cetara e parmigiana di alici
food.desc: Anchovies from the nearby fishing village of Cetara, layered like a parmigiana or dressed with colatura, the local fermented anchovy sauce.

places.name: Al Convento
places.note: The classic address for colatura di alici, in a former friary in the anchovy village.

places.name: Vicolo della Neve
places.note: Cooks the old Salerno repertoire, including anchovy and vegetable parmigiane.

places.name: Osteria Canali
places.note: Seasonal small plates featuring Cetara anchovies when they are landed.

food.name: Cuoppo di fritto misto
food.desc: Paper cone of deep-fried anchovies, squid, prawns and zeppoline dough balls, eaten hot while walking the seafront.

places.name: Friggitorie on Via Roma
places.area: Between the old town and the port
places.note: Takeaway fry shops turning out cones of seafood and battered vegetables all evening.

places.name: Lungomare Trieste kiosks
places.note: Kiosks under the palm trees, the local way to start a passeggiata.

places.name: Vicolo della Neve
places.note: Sit-down fritti and zeppoline in a room that has barely changed in decades.

food.name: Sfogliatella and Campanian pastries
food.desc: Crisp shell-shaped sfogliatella riccia filled with sweet ricotta and candied peel, plus lemon-scented coastal cakes.

places.name: Pasticceria Pantaleone
places.note: Historic Salerno pastry shop, a fixture for sfogliatelle and holiday sweets.

places.name: Pasticceria Romolo
places.note: Long-running local pasticceria with a strong reputation for classic Campanian cakes.

places.name: Sal De Riso
places.note: Celebrated coastal pastry chef; worth the bus ride for lemon delizia by the sea.

food.name: Limoncello and Concerto
food.desc: Amalfi lemon liqueur served ice cold after dinner, and Concerto, a dark herb-and-spice liqueur from Tramonti in the hills above town.

places.name: Vicolo della Neve
places.note: House digestivi after the calzoni, poured in the traditional way.

places.name: Bars on Via dei Mercanti
places.note: The old town's evening strip, where locals finish dinner with a chilled liqueur.

places.name: Sal De Riso
places.note: Sells coastal lemon liqueurs and cream versions alongside the pastries.

food.name: Cilento and Amalfi Coast wines
food.desc: Aglianico and Fiano from the Cilento hills, and the steep-terrace whites of the Costa d'Amalfi, both poured widely in the city.

places.name: Il Cavatappi
places.note: Wine-led kitchen with a good spread of Campanian bottles by the glass.

places.name: Osteria Canali
places.note: Short, well-chosen local wine list to go with the home cooking.

places.name: Cantine Marisa Cuomo
places.note: Famous cliffside winery with tastings of its terraced-vineyard whites; book ahead.

landmarks: Duomo di Salerno (Salerno Cathedral)
An 11th-century Norman cathedral above the tomb of St Matthew the Evangelist, entered through a colonnaded atrium of ancient Roman columns.
Castello di Arechi
A Lombard hilltop castle 300 metres above the city, its ramparts commanding the definitive panorama over Salerno's gulf and the Amalfi Coast.
Giardino della Minerva
A terraced medieval botanical garden created by physician Matteo Silvatico, teaching garden of Europe's first medical school, fragrant with healing plants and sea views.
Lungomare Trieste
Salerno's palm-lined seafront promenade, among Italy's most elegant, curving from the port toward the Amalfi Coast with benches facing the blue gulf.
Via dei Mercanti
The medieval main street threading the old town, a lively corridor of boutiques, churches and palazzi that has hummed with commerce for a millennium.
Complesso di San Pietro a Corte
The subterranean remains of Lombard prince Arechi II's eighth-century palace chapel, layered over a Roman bath complex beneath the old town.
Museo Archeologico Provinciale
The province's archaeology museum, treasuring a bronze head of Apollo hauled from the Gulf of Salerno by fishermen in 1930.
Pinacoteca Provinciale di Salerno
A palazzo gallery on Via dei Mercanti spanning Renaissance altarpieces to local masters, an intimate art pause amid the old town bustle.
Forte La Carnale
A 16th-century anti-Saracen watchtower guarding the seafront by the Irno river mouth, now a cultural venue with rooftop views along the coast.
Teatro Verdi
A gilded 1872 opera house with a horseshoe auditorium of four velvet-draped tiers, still staging opera and ballet in central Salerno.

train.note: No international trains. Salerno is a busy junction on the Tyrrhenian line, with Frecciarossa and Italo high-speed trains to Naples in 35 minutes and Rome in about two hours, plus regional services down the coast to Paestum and Reggio Calabria. The station is a short walk from the seafront and the ferry terminal. Booking opens around 120 days ahead.

bus.note: Coaches use the terminal beside the railway station. SITA Sud (https://www.sitasudtrasporti.it/) runs the Amalfi Coast buses from here to Amalfi and Positano - a spectacular but slow ride on a narrow cliff road, and very crowded in summer. FlixBus covers the long-distance Italian and European routes.

intl.to: Amalfi, Positano & Capri (Italy) - seasonal fast ferry, Apr-Oct
Capri, Ischia & the Amalfi Coast (Italy) - seasonal

ferry.note: There are no international sailings, but Salerno's Molo Manfredi terminal is the best way onto the Amalfi Coast in season - the boats to Amalfi and Positano avoid the traffic on the coast road entirely and take 35-70 minutes. Services run roughly April to October only and are cancelled in rough seas, so keep a bus fallback in mind.

half.name: Vietri sul Mare
half.blurb: The ceramics capital of the Amalfi Coast, minutes from Salerno, its majolica-domed church and tile-covered lanes bursting with colourful pottery workshops.
